runs.v: , mapping the subsurface moisture behind a failure. Can infrared technology detect roof leaks? Indirectly, yes: infrared thermography detects moisture by temperature differences, so it finds the wet insulation that water leaves behind rather than the breach itself, and it is especially effective on flat and low-slope roofs, residential or commercial, where water is difficult to track visually.

carries a higher heat capacity than dry insulation and cools more slowly after sunset, so an infrared camera reads the moisture-contaminated area as a warm anomaly, per Fluke and IIBEC infrared application guidance. Water has a higher thermal mass than dry roofing materials: in daytime the dry materials heat up quickly, then cool down rapidly after sunset, while wet insulation holds its heat as the roof cools. The scan locates the moisture intrusion, not the entry point itself, because water travels through the assembly and the wet area separates from the breach.

c.v: Is an infrared scan worth it?

runs.v: On a flat roof where water keeps coming back, usually yes: infrared inspections are non-destructive and cost-effective, and infrared thermal imaging can map moisture footprints across large roofs quickly where hand probing would open the membrane in dozens of places. Do infrared moisture meters work? An infrared camera measures surface temperature, not moisture, so an infrared roof moisture inspection pairs the camera with a moisture meter that reads the moisture trapped in the insulation directly. The scan also finds the wet insulation that small punctures from foot traffic and seam failures admit, often before water damage appears inside; pinpointing a pinhole in the membrane itself takes an electronic membrane test under ASTM D7877. Unlike a whole-house home inspection, this professional roof leak detection looks only at the roof assembly.

On some older Central Avenue and Main Street commercial blocks, the gravel or paver mass absorbs and releases heat uniformly and masks the wet-dry temperature difference, so where contrast runs low on a ballasted commercial building, a Newark Quality Roofing survey adds core-cut and calibrated moisture-meter checks, per ASTM and Fluke. ASTM C1153 also sets a dry surface, no appreciable precipitation in the roughly 48 hours prior, wind under roughly 15 mph, and a clear day followed by a clear night, per ASTM C1153 as applied through IIBEC and Fluke; infrared scanning should not be performed immediately after rain or heavy winds, when readings are unreliable. The wet-area contrast narrows to about 5°F in winter against 20°F in summer, so a low-contrast cold-weather scan carries more verification. Roofs here face extreme weather that increases maintenance needs: New Jersey's humid climate and seasonal coastal storms make reliable moisture detection more important, and routine roof maintenance prevents leaks and extensive damage.
